name: The Kurrajong of the English Garden

location.address: Giardino Inglese, Reggia di Caserta, Viale Douhet 2/a, 81100 Caserta

access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
story:
An Australian bottle tree stands thirty-five metres tall in a Bourbon queen's garden, roughly twice the height a kurrajong reaches at home. Brachychiton populneus grows across the dry eastern half of Australia, where most specimens top out somewhere between fifteen and twenty metres. The register puts this one at thirty-five, with three metres sixty around the trunk, which makes it an exceptional tree for the species by a wide margin.

Kurrajong belongs to the mallow family, alongside cotton, cacao and the baobab, and it shares the baobab's habit of storing water in a swollen trunk. Australian graziers cut the branches to feed stock through drought, the fibrous bark was worked into cord, and the seeds are edible once roasted. None of that has ever been asked of this one. It stands in the English Garden at the top of the Reggia's grounds, the informal twenty-three hectares laid out from 1786 for a queen who wanted a botanical collection rather than another parterre, and it has spent its whole life being watered by an aqueduct and looked at.

The Campania register credits it with about a hundred and fifty years. That figure is the register's own estimate rather than a ring count, and the national list carries the same trunk, the same height and no age at all.

name: The Himalayan Chir Pine of the English Garden

location.address: Giardino Inglese, Reggia di Caserta, Viale Douhet 2/a, 81100 Caserta

access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
story:
The chir pine is tapped for resin on Himalayan foothills from Pakistan to Nepal, and one of them grows in the garden of a Bourbon palace outside Naples. Pinus roxburghii is a tree of dry slopes between roughly 500 and 2,000 metres, where whole local economies run on it: resin for turpentine and rosin, timber for building, and needles swept up in quantity for fodder, fuel and bedding. Those needles are among the longest of any pine, up to thirty centimetres, carried in drooping bundles of three, so the crown reads looser and shaggier than any European pine standing near it.

This one is twenty-five metres tall with three metres fifty around the trunk. A Himalayan pine is not garden decoration, it is a collector's tree, and the English Garden spent much of the nineteenth century working as a botanical collection under Giovanni Gussone and later Nicola Terracciano, who filled it with species nobody in Campania had grown before. The queen it was built for in 1786 wanted a garden that would beat the other royal gardens of Europe, and the botanists who came after her kept buying.

The register puts the pine at about a hundred and fifty years and marks the number as an estimate. Nothing in this garden has been dated by counting rings, so read it as a period rather than a date.

name: The Turkey Oak of the English Garden

location.address: Giardino Inglese, Reggia di Caserta, Viale Douhet 2/a, 81100 Caserta

access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
story:
In a garden collected out of Australia, the Himalaya and California, this oak grows wild in the hills a few kilometres away. Quercus cerris is native across southern Europe and Asia Minor, and grand gardens of the nineteenth century planted it anyway, because it grows faster than almost any other oak and reaches size while the owner is still alive to see it. This one is thirty-five metres tall with three metres forty-five around the trunk.

It is easy to identify once you look down. The acorn cups are covered in long whiskery scales, shaggy as a thistle head, and the acorns take two seasons to ripen instead of one. The leaves are rough to the touch, deeply and irregularly cut, and many of them hang on brown into the winter.

What the tree has watched from this spot is the end of a dynasty. The English Garden was Bourbon royal property for its first seventy years, laid out from 1786 and stocked with imports for a queen. In 1860 the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies fell, and the palace and its grounds passed to the House of Savoy and then to the Italian state, which is who charges for the ticket today. The register's hundred and fifty years is an estimate rather than a measurement, so this oak may have arrived just before that change of ownership or just after it.

name: The Southern Magnolia of Piazza Carlo di Borbone

location.address: Piazza Carlo di Borbone, Reggia di Caserta, 81100 Caserta

access: Free. On the palace grounds at Piazza Carlo di Borbone, in front of the Reggia; open as part of the public square, no ticket needed to see it from the piazza.
transport: Caserta station faces the palace directly across the piazza.
story:
Four metres forty around the trunk is a great deal of magnolia, and this one asks nobody for a ticket. It grows on Piazza Carlo di Borbone, the elliptical square in front of the Reggia, rather than behind the wall of the English Garden up the hill, twenty-five metres tall and open to anyone at any hour.

Magnolia grandiflora comes from the warm southeastern United States and has been planted as a specimen tree across Europe since the middle of the eighteenth century, for two reasons. The leaves stay on all year, dark and leathery on top with a rust-coloured felt underneath that is worth turning one over to see. And the flowers are enormous, cream white, up to thirty centimetres across and scented of lemon, opening a few at a time through the summer rather than all at once, so the tree is never covered in them and never quite out of them either.

The building behind it has had a stranger life than the tree. By 1944 the palace was Allied headquarters in the Mediterranean, and on 29 April 1945 the surrender of German forces in Italy was signed inside it. The magnolia was well grown by then: the Campania register credits it with about a hundred and fifty years, an estimate rather than a recorded planting date, which would have made it roughly eighty years old on the morning of the signing.

best_time.label: May to July, when the white flowers open, up to thirty centimetres across and smelling of lemon

name: The Upright Osage Orange of the English Garden

location.address: Giardino Inglese, Reggia di Caserta, Viale Douhet 2/a, 81100 Caserta

access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
story:
The best bow wood in North America grows in a royal garden outside Naples. Maclura pomifera takes its English name from the Osage nation, whose bows were traded far beyond their own country, and the wood behind that reputation is heavy, springy and so rot-resistant that a fence post cut from it outlasts the fence. Before barbed wire, American farmers planted the tree in thorny hedgerows across thousands of miles of the Midwest.

The fruit is the reason to come in autumn. Each one is the size of a grapefruit, green, wrinkled like a brain, heavy enough to be worth not parking under, full of sticky white latex and eaten by almost nothing alive. One well-argued theory holds that its dispersers were the mastodons and giant ground sloths that disappeared from North America some thirteen thousand years ago, which would make every fruit dropped here an offer to a customer who no longer exists. They come down through September and October and lie where they land.

Two Osage oranges in this garden hold monumental status, and the register describes this one as the upright specimen: two metres sixty around the trunk, twenty-five metres tall, and about two hundred years old by the register's estimate. Taken at face value that puts it within thirty years of the garden's creation in 1786, which would make it one of the older residents of a collection built almost entirely out of foreigners.

best_time.label: September and October, when grapefruit-sized green fruit thump down and lie where they land

name: The Hackberry of the English Garden

location.address: Giardino Inglese, Reggia di Caserta, Viale Douhet 2/a, 81100 Caserta

access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
story:
Ancient writers put this tree forward as the lotus that made Odysseus's crew forget the way home. Celtis australis carries small dark fruit on long stalks, sweet and vaguely date-like when ripe, which is enough to keep the identification alive; a thorny North African shrub, Ziziphus lotus, has an equally old claim on the same story, and nobody has settled it.

The wood is not in dispute. Hackberry is hard and flexible in a way few Mediterranean broadleaves are, and Italian workshops turned it for centuries into tool handles, walking sticks, whip stocks and the long forks used for turning hay. It is also one of the standard shade trees of the Italian piazza, planted for a wide canopy and for roots that put up with being paved over.

This one has been asked to do neither job. Three metres fifty around the trunk and twenty-five metres tall, it stands in the English Garden among kurrajongs, redwoods and Himalayan pines, which is an odd room for a species most Italians walk past without looking up. The trees around it were shipped in from four continents for a queen who wanted a collection. The hackberry needed no shipping at all: the species grows wild across Italy and through the Mediterranean basin. The register gives it about two hundred years, an estimate rather than a count, which makes it one of the longer-standing things in a garden laid out from 1786.
